title: WHY EZEKIEL WAS CALLED “SON OF MAN” OVER 90 TIMES
paragraphs: WHY EZEKIEL WAS CALLED “SON OF MAN” OVER 90 TIMES
The title appears again.
And again.
And again.
Page after page, vision after vision, judgment after judgment, restoration after restoration, God addresses Ezekiel with the same startling phrase:
“Son of man.”
Not prophet.
Not priest.
Not servant.
Not chosen one.
Not messenger.
Son of man.
More than ninety times.
When modern readers encounter this repeated title, many skim over it without stopping. It feels ordinary. Familiar. Almost insignificant.
Yet hidden within those two words is one of the most profound revelations about human weakness, divine glory, humility, identity, and grace in all of Scripture.
Understanding why Ezekiel was called “Son of Man” does far more than explain a biblical phrase.
It explains us.
It explains how God works through broken people.
It explains why heaven’s greatest stories are never about human greatness.
And it explains why every scandal can become grace when Jesus enters the story.
The answer begins in exile.
Everything Ezekiel thought his life would become had collapsed.
Jerusalem was devastated.
The Temple was desecrated.
The nation was humiliated.
The people of God were scattered.
The future looked shattered.
Ezekiel himself was among the captives carried into Babylon.
He was a priest without a temple.
A spiritual leader without a nation.
A man watching everything sacred fall apart.
For many people, this would have been the end of the story.
But God specializes in beginning new chapters where everyone else sees endings.
That theme echoes through Scripture.
Joseph moved from prison to palace.
David moved from shepherd fields to the throne.
Peter moved from denial to restoration.
Paul moved from persecutor to apostle.
And Ezekiel moved from exile to prophet.
Because God rewrites everything.
The phrase translated “Son of Man” comes primarily from the Hebrew expression:
בֶּן־אָדָם
Ben-Adam.
Literally:
“Son of Adam.”
Or more naturally:
“Human being.”
“Mortal.”
“One belonging to humanity.”
The emphasis is not primarily on status.
It is on frailty.
Creatureliness.
Human limitation.
Dust.
The same Adam formed from the ground.
The same humanity affected by sin.
The same weakness every person carries.
Each time God says “Ben-Adam,” He is reminding Ezekiel of something critical.
“You are human.”
The prophet is receiving visions of heavenly chariots.
He is witnessing the glory of God.
He is seeing angelic beings unlike anything the world has ever imagined.
He is hearing divine decrees concerning nations.
He is being entrusted with revelation that would shape generations.
Yet every time divine glory increases, God simultaneously reminds Ezekiel of his humanity.
“Ben-Adam.”
Human one.
Mortal one.
Dust-born one.
Why?
Because revelation without humility destroys people.
Knowledge without humility corrupts.
Spiritual experiences without humility create pride.
Power without humility becomes dangerous.
God continually anchors Ezekiel in reality.
“You are seeing heavenly things, but you remain human.”
This pattern appears immediately in Ezekiel 2:1:
“And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.”
The Hebrew reads:
בֶּן־אָדָם עֲמֹד עַל־רַגְלֶיךָ
Ben-Adam, amod al-raglekha.
“Son of man, stand on your feet.”
The command is powerful.
Before Ezekiel can speak for God, he must understand who he is.
Not God.
Not divine.
Not the hero.
Not the center.
Only a servant.
The messenger is never greater than the message.
This truth feels especially important today.
Our culture celebrates self-exaltation.
Followers.
Influence.
Recognition.
Platforms.
Personal brands.
Many people secretly want God’s power while avoiding God’s humility.
But Scripture consistently reveals the opposite pattern.
The closer someone comes to God, the more aware they become of their own dependence.
Isaiah cried:
“Woe is me.”
Peter fell before Jesus saying:
“Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”
John collapsed “as dead” before the glorified Christ.
The truly godly do not become more impressed with themselves.
They become more impressed with God.
That is exactly what “Son of Man” was teaching Ezekiel.
But there is another layer.
A deeply emotional one.
A breathtaking one.
God repeatedly calling Ezekiel “Son of Man” was not merely a reminder of weakness.
It was also a reminder of relationship.
Notice what God did not call him.
He did not call him failure.
He did not call him exile.
He did not call him captive.
He did not call him disgrace.
He did not call him forgotten.
He called him what he truly was.
A human being known by God.
Many readers carry wounds from labels.
Divorced.
Addict.
Failure.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Broken.
The world loves assigning permanent identities to temporary chapters.
But God often speaks differently.
The Lord addresses Ezekiel according to reality, not shame.
Human.
Mortal.
Dependent.
Yet still chosen.
Still called.
Still useful.
Still loved.
The same God who acknowledged Ezekiel’s weakness also entrusted him with extraordinary purpose.
That matters.
Because God does not wait for perfection before using people.
He works through people who know they need Him.
The scandal is not that God uses imperfect people.
The scandal is that He has never used any other kind.
Then something astonishing happens when we move from Ezekiel into the New Testament.
The phrase “Son of Man” takes on a completely different dimension.
In Hebrew, Ezekiel is “Ben-Adam.”
In Greek, the New Testament phrase is:
Υἱὸς τοῦ Ἀνθρώπου
Huios tou Anthrōpou.
“Son of Man.”
And remarkably, this becomes Jesus’ favorite title for Himself.
More than any other designation.
More than Messiah.
More than King.
More than Son of David.
Jesus repeatedly identifies Himself as the Son of Man.
At first glance this seems strange.
Why would the eternal Son of God choose a title emphasizing humanity?
Because the Gospel is the story of God entering our condition.
The One Ezekiel saw in glory became flesh.
The eternal Word stepped into human history.
The Creator entered creation.
The Judge entered the courtroom.
The Shepherd entered the wilderness.
The Holy One entered our suffering.
Jesus became what we are so we could become what we could never be apart from Him.
Fully reconciled to God.
The title that reminded Ezekiel of human weakness becomes, in Christ, a declaration of divine redemption.
The Son of God became the Son of Man so sons and daughters of Adam could become children of God.
This is why the title carries such emotional weight.
Ezekiel was called “Son of Man” because he was merely human.
Jesus called Himself “Son of Man” because He willingly became human.
One title.
Two realities.
One highlighting humanity’s weakness.
The other revealing God’s love.
Together they tell the story of redemption.
The story reaches its climax in Daniel 7:13-14 where the prophet sees:
“One like a son of man.”
The Aramaic expression is:
כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ
Kevar Enash.
“Like a son of man.”
This figure approaches the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will never end.
Jesus repeatedly applies this prophecy to Himself.
The humble servant.
The suffering Messiah.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The eternal ruler.
The Son of Man who will return in glory.
Suddenly Ezekiel’s title becomes part of a much larger story.
Humanity’s weakness meets God’s redemption.
Dust meets glory.
Exile meets restoration.
Scandal meets grace.
And Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps that is why Ezekiel’s story still resonates thousands of years later.
Because most people know what exile feels like.
Not Babylonian exile.
Personal exile.
The exile of regret.
The exile of failure.
The exile of broken relationships.
The exile of dreams that died.
The exile of wondering whether God can still use your life.
Ezekiel’s answer is yes.
The God who spoke to a displaced priest beside a foreign river is still speaking today.
The God who called a captive into purpose still calls ordinary people.
The God who reminded Ezekiel of his humanity while filling him with divine purpose still does the same for us.
You may feel forgotten.
You may feel disqualified.
You may feel like your story has already been written.
But Scripture consistently tells another story.
A better story.
God is still writing.
The greatest danger is not weakness.
The greatest danger is believing weakness disqualifies you from grace.
Ezekiel was a son of man.
Jesus became the Son of Man.
And because of Christ, ordinary sons and daughters of Adam can become part of an extraordinary redemption story.
That is the Gospel.
That is why Ezekiel was called “Son of Man” more than ninety times.
Not to diminish him.
To position him correctly before the glory of God.
To remind him that power belongs to God.
To remind him that purpose comes from God.
To remind him that even dust can carry divine assignments.
And perhaps that reminder is exactly what many hearts need today.
You do not have to be impressive for God to use you.
You do not have to have a spotless past.
You do not have to erase every failure.
You simply need the grace found in Jesus Christ.
Someone scrolling through despair today may need this reminder more than you realize.
Because one shared article can reach a searching heart.
One act of support can become part of someone else's journey from darkness into light.
And one surrendered life in the hands of Christ can change eternity.
The same God who spoke to a son of man beside the rivers of Babylon is still calling ordinary people into extraordinary grace.
